name: Pindos
notes: Greece's mountain horse, from the Pindus range across Epirus, Thessaly and Macedonia - the Pindos Horse or Pindos Pony, the same animal either way. A pack, farm and trail horse from country where a cart could not go, and it carried ammunition through the mountains in the Greco-Italian war.

Bay leads, with chestnut a real minority and grey a visible quarter of the herd; black and brown come out of the same extension and agouti pool. Those are the colours the Greek breed sources name, in that order of emphasis.

Roan and a mild flaxen are both kept low. Roan is reported in supplementary breed material rather than measured, and flaxen is there so the occasional chestnut has a pale mane without it becoming a signature.

Cream, pearl, champagne, silver, mushroom, dun, every white pattern and the leopard complex are forced wild. This is a solid-coloured mountain landrace and nothing in the sources reaches to a pinto or a dilute.

No Pindos genotype survey exists. An academic source puts a historic census near 500 animals and the Greek breed organisation cites a larger 2019 registered figure; the difference is time and method, and rare is the defensible tier either way.
Tolerant both ways and modestly: the Pindus has hot dry summers and cold snowy winters, and a mountain landrace is sorted by both without specialising in either.

All disorders clear. The genetic-diversity work on Greek native breeds establishes the Pindos as a distinct population with high heterozygosity but reports no carrier frequency for anything on the panel, and borrowing from other Mediterranean or Balkan breeds would be a guess.

The narrow dark exceptionally hard hooves are the breed's clearest practical signature and are not modelled; nor are the cow hocks that help it find purchase, the thick mane, the long tail, its thrift on sparse forage, or its pack capacity.
